g.text: Cold audiences. Stop the scroll and earn attention. (20 new formats)
N1 Aesthetic Room Tour (Styled Space Walkthrough)
g.textArea:
What it is: A silent, music-led handheld/gimbal walkthrough of one beautifully styled room or home: opens on a 'pov: the life I want' / 'small bedrooms can still be beautiful' caption over a wide shot, glides past details (bed, lamp, shelves, textures), and closes on the full room with a 'shop the look' line.

Why it works: It sells the aspirational lifestyle, not the item; the viewer wants the whole room and the products come with it. Works for home decor, furniture and bedding brands with an influencer-styled space.

How to make one: 1) Style one room fully with your products (or partner with a home influencer whose room already looks great). 2) Shoot slow gimbal glides and detail close-ups in warm golden light, with a short aspirational POV caption on top. 3) Cut to trending calm music, end on the hero wide shot with 'shop the collection' or a price/offer line.

Closest format already on the board: Day In The Life / Satisfying B-roll - no person's routine or random b-roll here; the whole ad is a guided tour of a styled room as the aspiration.

What it is: The whole ad is a short animated story (Pixar-style 3D or hand-drawn 2D picture book) with a human or pet protagonist: opens on the character living the problem, middle shows failed fixes then discovering the product, close shows the happy 'after' and a product end card.

Why it works: Cartoon storytelling stops the scroll, lets you dramatize embarrassing or invisible problems (bloating, acne, a sick dog) without real actors, and is cheap to make with AI video.

How to make one: 1) Write a 30-60s first- or third-person story: problem moment, what they tried that failed, discovery of the product, life after. 2) Generate a consistent Pixar-style or storybook character and animate each beat as a scene, with captions/voiceover. 3) Show the real product clearly at the discovery beat and end on a product card with offer.

Closest format already on the board: Claymation / Talking Objects - Claymation is a different style and Talking Objects has the product or body part narrating; here an animated person/pet acts out a problem-to-solution story.

What it is: A cinematic manifesto: opens on a bold logo or one-word line, then a fast montage of many aspirational people/moments (or one protagonist in vignettes) runs under a single VO or word-by-word super that states what the brand believes, and closes on logo + tagline.

Why it works: Turns a commodity into an identity ('people like us use this'), building brand recall and a tribe; best for cold reach and to give the brand a point of view.

How to make one: 1) Write a 4-8 line belief statement about the buyer's identity, not the product (e.g. 'Your body needs it to perform, to recover, to embrace the moments'). 2) Cut 10-15 short, high-energy lifestyle/athlete clips (stock or shot), one line of the manifesto per clip as a centered super or VO. 3) Show the product only in 1-2 beats, end on logo + tagline.

Closest format already on the board: Goal / Dream Journey or Personal Story: those follow one real person's arc; this is a belief statement read over a montage of many people.

g.text: N4 Campaign Shoot Vlog (On Set BTS)
g.textArea:
What it is: Lo-fi phone vlog from the brand's own campaign/photo shoot: opens 'we're on set for our ... shoot', then handheld clips of models/founder changing, crew, lights, mood boards and between-take moments showing the new collection, closing on a final look or group shot.

Why it works: Shows a new collection on real bodies in an exciting insider context, so it reads as native content rather than a polished catalogue ad.

How to make one: 1) During any product photoshoot, have someone film vertical handheld BTS: setup, outfit changes, models laughing, shot review. 2) Add casual narrator captions ('we're on set for...', 'she wants to frame this one'). 3) Cut 30-60s, end on the best final look or a lineup of the pieces.

Closest format already on the board: Day In The Life / Try-On Haul - here the setting is the brand's own shoot and the collection is revealed through on-set BTS, not a creator's day or a solo try-on.

What it is: A 10-40s film-style micro story with a character, a setting and a small plot (a bellhop loads the bag, a man hunts the sea for his underwear, a kid's fingerprint becomes mom's necklace): the product is a prop inside the scene, there is no pitch or VO, and it ends on a title-card style logo.

Why it works: Feels like a film scene, not an ad, so it earns attention and brand intrigue; works for fashion, gifting and lifestyle products with a strong aesthetic.

How to make one: 1) Write a 3-beat scene (setup, small twist/action, payoff) where the product is the object the character wants or uses. 2) Shoot it like cinema: one location, styled cast, slow camera, natural sound or one music cue, no talking to camera. 3) End on a title card with the brand name (like a film title) instead of a hard offer.

Closest format already on the board: Scenarios / Day In The Life: those are creator-native or hypothetical; this is a scripted cinematic scene with a micro plot and a film title-card close.

g.text: N6 IRL Brand Stunt (Street Activation Recap)
g.textArea:
What it is: Documentary-style recap of a real-world stunt the brand staged: open on the strange public moment (posters with tear-off samples, costumed bellhops, a medieval troupe), middle shows passers-by reacting and engaging, close on the product reveal and brand card.

Why it works: Real-world spectacle feels like news, not an ad, and makes a small brand look big and culturally present.

How to make one: 1) Plan one cheap physical stunt tied to the product (sample tear-off posters, costumed staff handing it out). 2) Film it handheld/documentary style with real bystander reactions. 3) Cut to 15-30s: stunt -> reactions -> product reveal -> logo.

Closest format already on the board: Street Interviews - also filmed in public, but here the brand stages a stunt and films reactions instead of asking questions.

g.text: N7 Meme Caption Loop (Relatable Joke Clip)
g.textArea:
What it is: A 4-10s single-shot (or quick-montage) clip with one relatable meme-format caption ('Me cancelling my $900 dental surgery after...', 'When you know who the killer is but can't prove it yet', 'Forever girl who needs something in her arms to fall asleep'), no voiceover, product visible in frame; it ends when the loop ends.

Why it works: Reads as a meme post rather than an ad, so it gets shared and watched to the end; same build as Video Static, only the caption is a relatable joke instead of a product headline.

How to make one: 1) Film or source a 5-8s clip of someone (or a pet) using the product in a funny or relatable moment. 2) Write one 'Me when...' / 'When you...' caption that ties the joke to the product's benefit. 3) Burn it on in native TikTok/IG text style, no VO, and test several captions on the same clip.

Closest format already on the board: Reaction / Trend-Hijack (Borrowed Fame) - that borrows an existing viral clip or trend; here it is the brand's own simple clip with a meme caption. Structurally identical to Video Static, so merged as its meme-caption variant.

g.text: N8 POV Comedy Skit (Creator Plays the Roles)
g.textArea:
What it is: One creator acts out a relatable 'POV:' situation as characters (often playing both sides with outfit swaps): open on the POV caption, middle is quick comic scenes or back-and-forth dialogue where the problem plays out, close with the product as the in-story fix or punchline.

Why it works: Reads as native TikTok comedy, not an ad, so cold viewers watch to the end and the product lands as the joke's payoff.

How to make one: 1) Write a 'POV: you...' line around the exact pain your product fixes. 2) Film 4-8 short scenes on a phone; swap a shirt/prop to play the 'problem' person and the 'fixer'. 3) Put the product in as the punchline in the last third, then a one-line CTA.

Closest format already on the board: Scenarios - that opens on 'imagine if' and narrates; here the creator performs the scene as characters, skit-style.

What it is: An 'ASMR' labelled ad with little or no voiceover: opens on the title + close-mic packaging sound, then a run of tactile sound moments (crinkle, pump, pour, lather, spray, crunch) using the product, closing on a calm end shot with the product.

Why it works: Sound-led sensory content is watched as entertainment, holds attention without a pitch and makes the product feel premium and satisfying.

How to make one: 1) Pick 5-8 sound-rich actions with the product (opening, pouring, applying, using). 2) Record close to a mic in a quiet room, no music or talking, and add a persistent 'ASMR' title overlay. 3) End on product hero shot + brand; keep it 10-35s.

Closest format already on the board: Satisfying B-roll (Front-Splice) - that is only a short visual hook spliced before a normal ad; here the whole ad is a sound-first ASMR routine with no pitch.

What it is: The whole ad is an original catchy song about the product: open on 'Have you heard this song?', middle is karaoke-captioned lyrics carrying every benefit over a montage of people using it, close on a lyric that is the CTA.

Why it works: Melody makes benefits memorable and the lyric captions keep people watching; good for broad lifestyle products.

How to make one: 1) Write a 20-30s song whose lines are your benefits (AI music tools work). 2) Cut a montage of different people using the product, one shot per line. 3) Add karaoke-style lyric captions with a waveform; end on the brand name line.

Closest format already on the board: Satisfying B-roll / Product Demo - montage of use, but the original song is the script and the hook.

What it is: A food-creator style recipe video: opens on the finished, craveable dish/drink (or a 'best drink I ever made' hook), then shows the recipe built step by step with the product added as one ingredient (pack shot mid-way), and closes on the money shot / first bite.

Why it works: It looks like native recipe content people save and share, so the product gets screen time inside something useful instead of a pitch; ideal for consumables (powders, oils, drink mixes, sauces, supplements).

How to make one: 1) Pick a craveable, trending recipe (mocktail, s'mores bars, protein bites) where your product is a natural ingredient. 2) Open on the finished result, then shoot hands/creator assembling it step by step with a clear branded pack shot as the product goes in. 3) End on the bite/sip reaction or hero shot with recipe card text and a soft CTA.

Closest format already on the board: UGC How-To / Product Demo - those show how to use the product itself; here the ad is a recipe and the product is just one ingredient in a bigger dish.

What it is: A produced, multi-actor comedy scene with a script: open on a relatable or absurd setup (genre parody, office/home chaos, staff skit), middle escalates the gag with the product woven into the plot, close on the product as the punchline plus a benefit/offer card.

Why it works: Entertainment buys attention and brand memory; works for broad products where the problem can be exaggerated into a joke.

How to make one: 1) Pick one exaggerated problem moment or a genre to parody (zombie film, sitcom, therapy). 2) Shoot a 15-60s skit with 2+ actors and a clear setup -> escalation -> product punchline. 3) Close on a pack shot with one benefit line and the offer.

Closest format already on the board: Problem-Agitate-Solve - same problem->fix arc, but delivered as an acted comedy sketch with characters, not a pitch.

g.text: N13 Set Up With Me (Space Makeover)
g.textArea:
What it is: A 'come set up / reset with me' video: opens on a bare, messy or outdated space (stripped bed, empty wall, cluttered counter), the creator unpacks and installs or styles the product in quick satisfying steps, and it closes on a slow pan of the finished 'dream' space.

Why it works: The before-to-after build is satisfying to watch and lets the viewer picture the product in their own home; best for home decor, bedding, furniture, organizers and wall art.

How to make one: 1) Start on the space looking plain or tired (or the sealed package next to it) with a POV caption like 'the bed of my dreams'. 2) Film fast hands-on steps of putting the product in: fitting sheets, hanging the piece, placing items, with close-ups of texture and the logo tag. 3) End on a styled wide shot of the finished space with soft lighting or a cosy moment (candle, pet, lying down).

Closest format already on the board: Unboxing / Product Demo - Unboxing stops at the first open and Demo shows the product working; here the whole ad is installing the product into a room and revealing the transformed space.

What it is: A 6-10s frame-by-frame stop-motion of the real product and props (no clay, no people): opens on the product alone or a closed case, items pop in, stack, pack or swap frame by frame to build a flat lay or scene, and it closes on the finished arrangement with one line of copy.

Why it works: The jerky 'magic' motion stops the scroll and shows many features or bundle items in seconds with no talent; great cheap test for accessories, bundles, luggage, beauty kits and gifts.

How to make one: 1) Shoot top-down or locked-off on a clean backdrop; move the product and props a little between each photo. 2) Build a story in 40-80 frames: empty to full flat lay, unpacked to packed case, or one colourway swapping to the next. 3) Add one short headline ('Overpack. It fits.') and end on the finished arrangement with logo.

Closest format already on the board: Claymation - same frame-by-frame technique, but here it is the real product and props building a scene, not clay characters telling a story.

g.text: N15 Video Static (Caption Over Looping B-roll)
g.textArea:
What it is: A 5-20s ad that is basically a static ad that moves: one silent, lo-fi b-roll loop of the product (pour, stir, fizz, held bottle) with a single headline or meme caption burned on top (sometimes a few benefit tags or a short rolling caption list), no voiceover or presenter, ending on the same shot or a quick product/offer card.

Why it works: As cheap as a static image to make but plays as native video, so you can test dozens of headlines/angles fast; best for consumables and any product with a satisfying visual action.

How to make one: 1) Film one 5-10s phone clip of the product's best action (pour, mix, open, spray, wear) in natural light. 2) Burn one strong headline on top (question, POV, 'X for less than $Y', relatable line) plus 2-4 small benefit/price tags if needed. 3) Export 3-10 versions with different headlines on the same loop and let spend pick the winner.

Closest format already on the board: Text-Wall Story (Read-Along Still) - that is one still image carrying a long story; here it is a moving product loop with a single short headline, no story and no dwell-time read.

What it is: A voiceover (or punchy one-word captions) carries the pitch while the picture cuts every 1-2s to a different borrowed or absurd clip - archival B&W film, movie/anime moments, stunts, stock disasters, glitch zooms, cut-out meme stickers - with big word-by-word captions; the product only appears in a beat or two near the end, then a logo/CTA.

Why it works: The 'brainrot' edit pace makes it impossible to scroll past and lets a dry message (mechanism, comfort, ingredients) feel like entertainment; best for younger, meme-literate audiences and brands with a playful voice.

How to make one: 1) Write a tight 20-45s VO or caption script for the product's one key claim (problem -> mechanism -> product). 2) Cut a visual every 1-2s that literally or absurdly illustrates each word (archival clips, movie/anime moments, stock disasters, stunts), with glitch/zoom transitions and bold word-by-word captions. 3) Land the product in the last 5-8s (founder or hand holding it) and end on logo + one-line CTA.

Closest format already on the board: Reaction / Trend-Hijack (Borrowed Fame) - that borrows one existing viral clip or trend and reacts to it; here dozens of unrelated borrowed/absurd clips are spliced under your own VO as pure edit style.

g.text: N17 Absurdist Visual Gag (One Surreal Shot)
g.textArea:
What it is: A single surreal, impossible staged image held for 6-10s: open mid-scene on the weird visual, a small pull-back or twist reveals the full gag, close with at most one caption and the product as the prop.

Why it works: Cheap pattern-interrupt that stops the scroll on pure curiosity; best for brand-world building and retargeting creative refresh.

How to make one: 1) Brainstorm one impossible image that ties to the product (bath in a truck bed, product playing on an old TV). 2) Shoot it cinematically in one location, 6-10s, with a slow reveal. 3) Add one short caption or none; keep the product visible but secondary.

Closest format already on the board: Satisfying B-roll (Front-Splice) - also a visual scroll-stopper, but this is a staged surreal joke that IS the whole ad, not a splice before the pitch.

What it is: The brand owner vlogs explaining the product in the shop, then delivers/donates it to a community hero group (e.g. a police K9 unit), filming the handover, the recipients' thank-yous and why it matters, ending on the brand card.

Why it works: Goodwill and a respected recipient make the brand likeable and quietly endorse the product's usefulness.

How to make one: 1) Pick a sympathetic recipient that genuinely needs the product (rescue shelter, nurses, K9 unit, coaches). 2) Film the owner explaining the product, then the real handover and reactions in one continuous vlog. 3) Close with the recipients' thanks and a soft brand/offer card.

Closest format already on the board: Gift Reaction Reveal - that focuses on one person's emotional unwrap; this is an owner vlog of a donation to a community group, with the product explained along the way.

What it is: Friends at a table play a real party game (Wavelength dial, red flag/green flag) re-skinned with prompts about the product category: open on the game title, middle is 1-2 min of banter and laughs as they debate prompts, close with the product as the answer/punchline.

Why it works: Long, fun watch time and natural objection-handling through banter; great for awkward or taboo categories.

How to make one: 1) Pick a known game format and write 8-10 prompts about your niche's habits and objections. 2) Film 2-3 friends playing unscripted with a light brand bug on screen. 3) Cut to the best moments; let the product win the last prompt.

Closest format already on the board: Episodic Series / Social Show - also show-like, but this is one self-contained game round with category prompts, not a recurring series.

g.text: N20 Prank Skit (Product Used On A Friend)
g.textArea:
What it is: Lo-fi handheld prank: open on a caption like 'lasering my roommate's stuff' or sneaking up on a sleeping friend, middle is the product used on the unaware victim (often a quick montage), close on the victim's reaction or 'what should I do next?'.

Why it works: Prank content is natively shareable and demos the product in a fun, real-world way for cold audiences.

How to make one: 1) Pick a harmless prank only your product can do (engrave their things, blast cold air on them). 2) Film handheld, secretive, 15-60s; montage several 'victims' or items. 3) End on the reaction and a comment-bait question.

Closest format already on the board: Product Demo Ads - shows the product working, but framed as a prank on a friend with a reaction payoff.
